did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens with a repetition of the word “return”: “If you return, Israel ... return,” emphasizing that returning to the LORD also involves removing detestable things and abandoning idolatry.

Did you know? Jeremiah uses an agricultural image to describe repentance: “Break up your unplowed ground” — prepare the soil, and do not sow among thorns. This portrays preparing the heart to receive what is good.
Did you know? The command “Circumcise yourselves to the LORD” is not limited to an outward act; it adds, “Remove the foreskins of your hearts” — a call for inner transformation.
Did you know? When the threat is announced, Judah and Jerusalem are commanded to blow the trumpet, declare a state of emergency, and gather in the fortified cities.
Did you know? The enemy is described as coming “from the north,” and the prophet also portrays it as a lion emerging from its lair and as a destructive force bringing “great destruction.”

Did you know? Even when the enemy is already approaching from Dan and from the hills of Ephraim, the call to Jerusalem is still: “Wash the evil from your heart” — cleansing the heart is presented as a condition for salvation.
Did you know? Jeremiah describes the people as not knowing the LORD: “They are skilled in doing evil, but they do not know how to do good” — they are clever in doing evil, but not in doing good.

Did you know? In his vision of destruction, Jeremiah sees the land as “formless and empty,” the heavens without light, the mountains trembling, and the birds fleeing — a picture of complete desolation in both nature and human settlement.
Did you know? Although the land is described as desolate, the LORD emphasizes: “Yet I will not destroy it completely” — the destruction will be severe, but it will not be total annihilation.
Did you know? Jerusalem tries to rely on clothing, jewelry, and makeup, but the prophet declares that outward beautification will not save her: “You beautify yourself in vain.”
